subtype: Approach: throwing everything in the bag just in case [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Hemant, and I sit next to Gurpreet in Class 6. He never checks the timetable; every book he owns goes into the bag, every day. By the second period he was leaning forward like an old man, and on the stairs he held the railing. Then the teacher asked for the English notebook. He dug past the atlas, the drawing file and a spare geometry box, pulling out crumpled sheets before he found it. The whole class waited, and he went red. At lunch he rubbed his shoulder, and when the strap slipped I saw the red marks.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet dig past before he found the English notebook?
qa.a: He dug past the atlas, the drawing file and a spare geometry box.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet have felt while the whole class waited?
qa.a: Embarrassed; he went red while everyone watched him search. 😔

qa.q: What other approach could Gurpreet try, and why would it work better?
qa.a: He could read the timetable and pack only tomorrow's books, since a light bag is easier to carry and a neat bag is easier to search. A short checklist at the door would also help.

qa.q: How does Hemant see Gurpreet's habit?
qa.a: Hemant sees a plan that costs Gurpreet comfort and time, and seems concerned rather than mocking, since he notices the strap marks and how the class waited.

grounding: A child keeps every book in the bag to avoid checking the timetable, and it becomes heavy and messy so the notebook is still hard to find.

subtype: Approach: throwing everything in the bag just in case [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday. Vaibhav stuffed every book he owned into his bag. "Now I never have to check the timetable," he told his grandfather, Jagdish. The zip only just closed.
Wednesday. On the walk to school he kept shifting the bag from one shoulder to the other. By the gate there was a red line across his shoulder.
Friday. In the Science period, Ma'am asked for the lab notebook. Vaibhav dug through fourteen books, an atlas and a broken ruler. By the time he found it, the class had copied the diagram and moved on. That afternoon Dada Jagdish, waiting at the gate, carried the bag home, frowning at its weight.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav dig through in the Science period?
qa.a: Fourteen books, an atlas and a broken ruler.

qa.q: How was Vaibhav feeling on Friday as he dug through the bag?
qa.a: He was probably flustered and embarrassed, falling behind while the class moved on.

qa.q: What would you change first in Vaibhav's approach?
qa.a: Check the timetable each evening and pack only that day's books; carrying everything made the bag heavy and the notebook harder to find.

qa.q: How does Dada Jagdish see the bag?
qa.a: Dada Jagdish frowns at its weight as he carries it, so he seems worried about how heavy it is for Vaibhav.

grounding: Shows a boy carrying every book to avoid checking the timetable, until the bag hurts his shoulder and he still cannot find the right notebook.

subtype: Approach: throwing everything in the bag just in case [Pitfall]
passage: Kunal, why is your bag bulging like a pumpkin? Sit, and let your Mehak Nani tell you about your Mama, Sameer. When he was ten, he decided checking the timetable was a waste of time. So he carried everything: every book, every notebook, even his old drawing book. Every morning he went up the lane to school bent forward like an old man. His shoulders ached so badly he couldn't lift his arms to bowl in the evenings. And the funny part? One day his teacher asked for his English notebook, and he couldn't find it among twenty others. He got a remark in his diary for 'no homework'. And he had done it!

qa.q: What did Sameer's teacher ask for?
How might young Sameer have felt when he got a remark for 'no homework'?
qa.a: He likely felt frustrated and unfairly treated, since he had actually done the homework but couldn't find it.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have saved Sameer his aching shoulders and the remark?
qa.a: Checking the timetable and packing only the day's books; carrying everything hurt his shoulders and buried the notebook.

qa.q: How might Sameer's teacher have seen the missing notebook?
qa.a: The teacher only saw homework that wasn't handed in, so it looked like none was done, though Sameer had done it.

grounding: Illustrates a boy who carries all his books to skip checking the timetable, ending up with aching shoulders and a notebook lost in the mess.
